title: Birth Order: So nice, we did it twice
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck re-record their earlier 'Birth Order' episode (their second time doing this, after the Black Holes episodes) and survey the history of birth order as a theory of personality. They cover Francis Galton's 1874 Royal Society study, Alfred Adler's individual psychology and family constellation idea, the dethroning trauma, Adler's sibling-by-sibling traits, the 1983 Angst and Ernst critique, Frank Sulloway's 1996 Born to Rebel and its critics including Judith Rich Harris, the 2015 Damian and Roberts studies finding little birth order effect, and James Zinck's SAT and IQ argument. They close with a listener email about Francis Kelsey and a note about the hosts' own siblings.

segments.title: Tour promo
segments.summary: Promotion for the hosts' final live shows of the year in Orlando, Atlanta, and Nashville, with tickets via the tour link.

segments.title: Rerun introduction
segments.summary: Hosts explain this is a re-recording of an episode they already made, the second time they have done this, after the Black Holes episodes.

segments.title: Opening banter and sibship
segments.summary: Banter about the term sibship (total siblings in a family) and high, low, and midsib ship labels, then a note that birth order is a long-debated idea that has been presented, refuted, and revived.

segments.title: Traditional birth order traits
segments.summary: Chuck describes the popular stereotypes: firstborns as bossy and perfectionist, middle children as peacemakers, youngest as adventurous. Josh notes only children resemble firstborns and that selection and confirmation bias keep the idea alive, comparing it to a horoscope.

segments.title: Francis Galton and the Royal Society study
segments.summary: Galton, a polymath and Darwin's half cousin, studied 99 Royal Society members in English Men of Science and found most were firstborn, only, or early middle-born. Galton's conclusion about elder sons' advantages in nurture and nourishment is read aloud.

segments.title: Recap of Galton's view
segments.summary: Chuck recaps Galton's point that the oldest child gets companionship with parents, early responsibility, and better infant nourishment, and the hosts find it not unreasonable.

segments.title: Alfred Adler and individual psychology
segments.summary: Adler, a colleague of Freud, developed individual psychology, including the family constellation and lifestyle concepts. He argued that being dethroned by a younger sibling was a trauma shaping personality, and that children in the same family do not grow up in the same environment.

segments.title: Adler's sibling position traits
segments.summary: Adler's traits for oldest, second, and middle children: oldest children feel responsible and act as parents, second children compete with and may rebel against the older sibling, and Adler's own relationship with his older brother Sigmund is discussed.

segments.title: Middle, youngest, and only children per Adler
segments.summary: Middle children may feel forgotten and seek belonging outside the family, which the hosts contrast with the people-pleaser stereotype, and Chuck shares his own family experience. Youngest children are described as more adventurous, and Adler's claim about successful youngest children drawn from the Bible and fairy tales is criticized as unscientific. Only children are described as little kings and queens.

segments.title: Mid-century acceptance and the 1983 Swiss critique
segments.summary: Birth order ideas were widely accepted through the 1920s to 1980s. In 1983 Swiss psychologists Jules Angst and Cecil Ernst reviewed about 1,500 studies, found methodological flaws, and called the theory post hoc, showing how explanations could be fitted to any result.

segments.title: Sulloway, Darwin, and Lyle
segments.summary: Frank Sulloway's professor linked Darwin's later-born rebelliousness to Charles Lyle's firstborn conservatism. Sulloway began research in 1970, and the hosts note his work overlapped with the Swiss critique.

segments.title: Sulloway's Born to Rebel and niche theory
segments.summary: Sulloway's 1996 book Born to Rebel argues birth order matters because each child occupies a niche defined by size, status, and power in the family, with a Darwinian struggle for parental affection. Firstborns align with authority and parents; later-borns use low-power strategies such as humor.

segments.title: Sulloway's historical database
segments.summary: Sulloway built a database of 6,566 historical figures across 121 political and scientific upheavals and claimed birth order outweighs 256 other factors. His examples, including Mussolini, Stalin, Marx, Darwin, Gandhi, Lincoln, Newton, and Einstein, are criticized as reductive.

segments.title: Reception of Born to Rebel and Judith Rich Harris critique
segments.summary: Born to Rebel became a bestseller and was widely criticized, including by Judith Rich Harris, who argued peers shape personality more than parents. Harris's sharp quote about the originator's evidence is cited. The hosts note the idea persists in parenting and psychology sites.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode sponsor break.

segments.title: 2015 large studies find little birth order effect
segments.summary: Damian and Roberts of the University of Illinois ran 2015 studies, one with 377,000 US high school students and one with about 20,000 students in Europe, finding little to no functional relation between birth order and personality. They criticized between-family designs and sacred cows such as gender differences and the five-year sibling gap.

segments.title: Zinck SAT and IQ theory and snapshot bias
segments.summary: Hosts discuss a small IQ difference favoring firstborns and James Zinck's SAT analysis predicting score rises and falls from the baby boom birth order pattern, which came true around 1980. Zinck's teaching-opportunity explanation is discussed, and the hosts warn of the perfect age compound: snapshot studies of siblings at different ages can mislead.

segments.title: Hosts' takeaway
segments.summary: Chuck concludes birth order is likely one factor among many in personality. Josh notes listener mail will follow.

segments.title: Listener mail: Francis Kelsey follow-up
segments.summary: Listener Katie writes that her sister Sarah admires FDA hero Francis Kelsey and thanks the show for the short on her. The hosts invite listeners to share sibling stories by email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and iHeartRadio production note.
